title: Breaking away from your idols
summary: Wilson explains how Fats, Hines and Tatum were his idols and a player must eventually trust his own sound.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: But eventually, it will come out -- the writing will come out pure, clear, loud and clean. If you just keep trying and don't back away from it, as over a period of time they will, so I think a young player, when they are developing an improvising style of your own. Because ideas do come to you, and of course the safe thing is -- we all start out idolizing someone. I remember Fats was my first idol, and then Hines and then Art.

And to break away from that, at a certain point, you must break away from that and let your own musical sense tell you what to try for, instead of the stuff you learned from your idols. That takes a little courage -- because you know when you've been copying a successful guy, and you know that's good. What you learn from, and you don't know whether your own stuff, whether you should go back to playing like so and so, when you start on your own.

But it takes a little courage to get that image of your idol, because you can imitate people, but you find that when you do it, you've got a picture of them playing in your mind, you learn a solo off a record, if you're a saxophone player, you can learn Fats's solos off a record, and then have a picture of Fats playing. But you get that picture out of your mind and just let your own ear take over and listen to your drummer and your bass and piano, and something
will come there, too. But you can't back away from it because that's you, and you got to let the chips fall where they may.

You may not be another Charlie Parker or another Art Tatum, but that's you -- and that's your greatest asset, even though it may not be the best. If it's you, it's very satisfying, it's as satisfying almost as if it was the best.
Yeah, when they hear something and say, 'Who is that?'

That's so right. Like maybe Tchaikovsky Beethoven is no , but I'm sure it must have been rewarding for him to write music and hear that symphony play it. But he knows what he is, and what music is in his soul, you hear it when you sit in the concert hall and listen to it. And those bases play all that stuff, those woodwinds, hit those diminished-- chrcds, and , you hear what was in his soul. It comes out in the violins.

What it is, you hear it. It may not be, as I said, it may not be Beethoven or Brahms, but you hear it. When he wants to give clarinet, you hear it and then the oboe and the sum total of it, and he doubles up and plays maybe schmaltzy once in awhile when he wants that effect, that romantic feeling, and then the rest. That's what a musician is.

As long as it sounds okay to you -- because everybody isn't going to be a Beethoven, you know; it's impossible. Or everybody is not going to be a Louis Armstrong or an Art Tatum. But as long as you are you, you'll have it made.
